headline: High-risk default interaction: LangGraph can write/read shared state and run tools while langchain4j may ingest content without isolation, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LangGraph can expose application-defined files, stdin/stdout, and developer-defined tools, while langchain4j is a general LLM framework with no isolation or provenance controls shown. A shared workspace or copied outputs could let attacker-controlled content from one agent steer the other. The pairwise pathway is plausible but not directly documented, so I choose medium over low.
conditions: IF both agents exchange text through a shared file or stdout/stderr channel
IF the orchestrator feeds one agent's output into the other's prompt without sanitization
mitigations: Add a strict delimiter and provenance tag to all inter-agent messages
Disable file-based handoff between the agents
Require human review before copying outputs across agents
requires-engineering: add content filtering for prompt-injection markers
requires-engineering: isolate each agent in separate workspaces

B_data_leakage.rationale: LangGraph explicitly handles model-provider API keys and can read/write application-defined files with broad network egress, while langchain4j has no documented filesystem isolation or data-class limits. If shared state contains secrets, either agent could surface them in outputs or send them onward. The evidence is indirect, so I rate this medium rather than high.
conditions: IF shared workspace files contain secrets or customer data
IF either agent is configured to include file contents in prompts or tool calls
mitigations: Move secrets out of shared files immediately
Restrict both agents to separate directories
Rotate any API keys present in shared state
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent access controls on the workspace
requires-engineering: redact sensitive fields before any handoff

C_capability_conflict.rationale: LangGraph can write the filesystem, execute shells, spawn subprocesses, and use broad network egress; langchain4j has no stated write or coordination limits. In a shared directory or mutable graph state, concurrent writes and tool actions can collide and corrupt artifacts. Because LangGraph's default orchestration is stateful and self-isolation is none, I escalate to high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or graph-state store
IF either agent modifies files that the other reads during the same run
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working directory
Serialize writes with a lock file or queue
Disable shell execution for nonessential steps
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency checks on shared state
requires-engineering: separate mutable git or database targets per agent

D_cascading_error.rationale: LangGraph is designed as a graph of nodes where each node may itself be an agent, so it can pass one agent's output directly into another step. Langchain4j is a general LLM framework and may emit unverified text that LangGraph treats as authoritative unless the developer adds checks. That default chaining makes cascading errors likely and potentially irreversible.
conditions: IF LangGraph routes langchain4j output into a downstream action node
IF no verification or schema validation is inserted between the agents
mitigations: Insert schema validation between agents
Require citations or structured outputs before acting
Add a human approval step for external actions
requires-engineering: add confidence thresholds before tool execution
requires-engineering: log and replay intermediate outputs for audit

E_compliance.rationale: LangGraph explicitly handles model-provider API keys and broad network egress, while langchain4j is a customer-support framework with no residency or retention controls shown. If regulated data is placed into LangGraph's graph state or sent through its tools, compliance obligations can diverge from the other agent's undocumented handling. The mismatch is plausible but not directly evidenced, so medium fits.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in LangGraph graph state
IF either agent sends that data to a model provider or external API
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared graph state
Document retention and deletion rules for both agents
Route sensitive workloads to approved endpoints only
requires-engineering: add residency-aware routing
requires-engineering: implement data-class specific retention controls
